### Part A - Creating Data Frames
```{r}
# TODO: Create three vectors of equal length (5 students): 
# name (character): "Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"
# age (numeric): 20, 21, 19, 22, 20
# passed (logical): TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Combine name, age, and passed into a data frame called students
# using data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
# Print students
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Check the type of the "name" column using typeof(students$name) and class(students$name)
typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)
```
```{r}
# TODO: Now create a SECOND data frame called courses directly, without separate vectors first, using data.frame() with these columns:
# course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103")
# units = c(3, 3, 2)
# instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)
courses
```
##### Question #1

##### You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline.
##### Both approaches produce the same kind of object.
##### In your own words, explain why data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length, and what error you would expect if they didn’t.

Answer: A data frame is a rectangular grid of data where the columns are variables and the rows are individual observations. This means that every column must have exactly the same number of rows as all the other columns. Passing vectors of different lengths would throw an error because it cannot construct a balanced, even table.

##### Question #2

##### A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.”
##### Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?

Answer: Since list can contain elements of different data types (character, numeric, logical etc) in its different components, whereas each individual vector (or column) has to contain strictly items of a single, uniform data type. A data frame is basically a list with a number of vectors of equal length . This means that columns of different types can be next to each other, and the data stays internally consistent .


```{r}
students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
```

##### Question #3

##### students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects.
##### Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.

Answer: studentsage extracts the column as a basic numeric vector, whereas students["age"] extracts it as a subsetted data frame container (a single-column data frame). This parallels what we saw with lists: single brackets ([]) preserve the container type (returning a sub-list or sub-data frame), while double brackets ([[]]) or the dollar sign ($) extract the underlying content directly.

##### Question #4

##### In df-multiple-conditions, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19) before that combined result is used to filter rows.
##### What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

Answer: The & operator is an element-wise logical AND . It compares the boolean value of passed == TRUE and age > 19 for each individual student row by row and produces a single combined logical vector of TRUE/FALSE values. Using | (OR) instead of & (AND), the filter would return any student that satisfies either condition, rather than requiring them to satisfy both conditions at the same time, resulting in a larger subset of rows.

##### Question #5

##### Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name).
##### Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.

Answer: R produces descriptive statistical summaries tailored to each data type: for numeric columns (age), it calculates summary metrics like the minimum, maximum, median, mean, and quartiles; for logical columns (passed), it counts the total frequencies of TRUE and FALSE values; and for character columns (name), it simply reports the length, class, and mode rather than statistics. A mean wouldn't make sense for the name column because strings/text cannot be mathematically averaged.

##### Question #6

##### str() and summary() both describe a data frame, but they show different information.
##### Based on what you observed, when would str() be more useful to you than summary(), and vice versa?

Answer: str() is more useful when you want to quickly inspect the underlying data types, internal storage structure, and initial preview of every column at a glance. Conversely, summary() is more useful when you want to analyze data distributions, check for missing values, and view analytical summary statistics (like means and quartiles) for numeric and logical variables.

##### Question #7

##### After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from df-logical-filter (students$passed == TRUE)?
##### Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.

Answer: No. You could not run that specific filter because the passed column was completely removed from the data frame, meaning R would return an error stating that the object/column cannot be found. This highlights why tracking a data frame’s changing structure is vital: running subsequent scripts or filters dependent on columns that were previously dropped will break your code.

##### Question #8

##### order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions.
##### Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).

Answer: The order() function evaluates the age column and returns the integer index positions of the rows sorted from youngest to oldest (e.g., row indices 3, 1, 2, 5, 4). When placed inside the row index position of students[index_vector, ], R reorganizes the entire data frame by pulling and re-sequencing all columns together according to that exact new row index order.

### Part E - Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

# TODO: Add a new column "average" to grades that holds the mean of
# midterm and final for each student. Hint: (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
grades
```
```{r}
# TODO: Print only the rows of grades where remarks is "Failed",
# showing just the name and average columns.
# Hint: grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```
##### Question #9

##### Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?”
##### Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.

Answer: To investigate this question using lab tools, you could first create new calculated columns: one measuring the score difference or drop between the midterm and final (grades$midterm - grades$final), and another indicating overall performance. Next, you could sort the data frame using order() based on the size of the score drop or sort by low midterm scores. Finally, you could inspect the sorted tables to see whether students with failing remarks consistently cluster around large grade drops or low initial midterms.

### Conclusion
A data frame is a two-dimensional, tabular data structure in R made up of equal-length columns where each column can maintain a different data type. It directly relates to vectors as its building blocks and functions essentially as a list of equal-length vectors. Because it seamlessly blends mixed data types with a clean row-and-column layout, it serves as R’s primary and most versatile structure for handling real-world datasets.
